answer: A registry can tie each identity to one karst cave chamber, charted for that holder alone. The holder lowers a willow sounding rod and files the echo time; the registry seals the next sounding point with that echo, so soundings chain one by one and no rod serves two chambers. Each sample is ferried to the wharf lab, where a drip-water assay checks the mineral fingerprint; a copied echo fails, since no two chambers share a drip pattern. One chamber costs $380 plus 26 field hours; 5,000 clones would need 5,000 chambers, $1.9 million, and 130,000 field hours, and no bulk order maps a second cave.
